record.title: OpenAI says it will honor a shared robots.txt preference signal for AI training
record.summary: OpenAI announced on 30 October 2026 that it will honor a shared robots.txt signal for website operators to express preferences about using their content for generative-AI training, with implementation planned in the coming months. The referenced IETF document is an individual Internet-Draft, not an IETF-endorsed standard. It defines a path-specific policy token using existing robots.txt group syntax; it does not itself create a crawler directive or enforce a preference. No implementation, adoption by other providers, or change to training-data collection is established.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: OpenAI announced on 30 October 2026 that it will honor a shared robots.txt signal for AI-training preferences and aims to implement it in the coming months.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The referenced draft defines the __usage_ai-training policy token in ordinary robots.txt groups, allowing path-specific preferences about use for generative-AI training while leaving existing crawler rules unchanged.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The IETF Datatracker classifies the document as an active individual Internet-Draft and states that it is not endorsed by the IETF and has no formal standing in the IETF standards process.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The sources do not establish that OpenAI has deployed the signal, that other providers honor it, that it creates a legal obligation, or that it has changed what content is collected or used for training.

evidence_gaps.description: The only inspected implementation commitment is OpenAI's statement that it plans to implement the signal in coming months; no deployed behavior or support by other providers was found.
The referenced text is an individual draft with no IETF endorsement or formal standards-process standing; its future working-group status is unknown.
No evidence links the announcement or draft to changes in crawling, content inclusion, training datasets, or publisher outcomes.

brief.importance_rationale: If adopted by web publishers and multiple AI providers, a shared training-preference signal could make content-use choices materially easier to express across services and reduce per-provider rule maintenance. The present record is capped at meaningful because the cited mechanism remains an individual Internet-Draft, OpenAI has not yet implemented it, and no provider uptake or data-use effect is measured.
limitations: The IETF Datatracker explicitly identifies the document as an individual Internet-Draft with no IETF endorsement or formal standing in the standards process.
OpenAI says implementation is planned in the coming months; this review found no deployed implementation or conformance test.
The token communicates a usage preference. The draft states that it is not a crawling directive; it does not itself establish legal enforceability or guarantee provider compliance.
No evidence was inspected showing adoption by other providers, changes to training-data collection, or effects on publishers or model training.
brief.summary: OpenAI announced on 30 October 2026 that it will honor a shared robots.txt signal for website operators to express preferences about using their content for generative-AI training, with implementation planned in the coming months. The referenced IETF document is an individual Internet-Draft, not an IETF-endorsed standard. It defines a path-specific policy token using existing robots.txt group syntax; it does not itself create a crawler directive or enforce a preference. No implementation, adoption by other providers, or change to training-data collection is established.

technical.claimed_result: OpenAI says the common signal will reduce separate provider-specific rule maintenance and that it plans to honor the signal after implementation in the coming months.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official OpenAI post and IETF Datatracker record demonstrate that OpenAI announced support for the signal and that the individual draft defines the described robots.txt token and semantics.
technical.implementation_status: Not yet demonstrated. OpenAI says it aims to implement the signal in the coming months; no release or live crawler test was found.
technical.mechanism: The individual draft uses a policy-token group in robots.txt—User-Agent: __usage_ai-training—to express a preference for or against generative-AI training on matched paths. It preserves existing product-token crawler rules and introduces no new robots.txt directive syntax. The draft says consumers may use the preference to inform crawling but the token itself is not a crawling directive.
technical.regime: Website operators expressing preferences about generative-AI training through robots.txt; one company's implementation commitment tied to an individual standards-track draft, as described by primary sources on 30 October 2026.
technical.reproducibility: The source text and draft are publicly inspectable; no implementation artifact or behavior was available to reproduce.
technical.strongest_baseline: OpenAI describes the prior approach as website operators maintaining separate rules for individual providers. No measured baseline for publisher effort or provider compliance was inspected.

brief.title: OpenAI says it will honor a shared robots.txt preference signal for AI training
brief.why_it_matters: A common signal could reduce the need for website operators to maintain separate training-preference rules for each provider and make a content-use preference easier to communicate across services. The current evidence establishes an OpenAI commitment and a draft mechanism, not implementation, broad provider uptake, legal force, or changed data practices.
